    Getting Started with conformeR

    Justine Leclerc and Christof Seiler

    conformeR-introduction.Rmd

    Overview

    LEMUR fits a low-dimensional embedding and assigns each cell to a neighborhood when they share a similar response to a given contrast and gene. Because this assignment is itself the output of a fitted model, it inherits sampling variability: refit the model on a slightly different draw of cells, and the neighborhood boundaries shift. conformeR wraps this neighborhood construction step in a conformal prediction layer so that this variability can be quantified rather than ignored.

    It provides two complementary views of that uncertainty:

    • Conformal selection asks, for a given gene, which cells can we confidently say belong to the affected neighborhood? It returns a data-driven subset of cells with a guaranteed bound on the proportion of false inclusions.
    • Conformal clustering asks the finer-grained question, for each cell, how uncertain are we about its neighborhood assignment? It returns a prediction set of plausible neighborhoods per cell, which can contain zero, one, or several labels.

    Why this matters. A single LEMUR fit gives you one particular neighborhood assignment, with no way to tell how much of it would survive resampling. conformeR turns that single assignment into a statement with a formal, finite-sample coverage guarantee.

    A caveat: the guarantee assumes true labels

    The coverage guarantees behind conformal prediction are proven under the assumption that the training and calibration sets carry the true neighborhood label for each cell. That assumption is exactly what motivates reaching for conformal prediction here in the first place — but it is also never satisfied in practice: we do not observe the true neighborhood membership of any cell. What we have instead is LEMUR’s own predicted neighborhood assignment, which we use as a proxy label for both training and calibration. That proxy is a noisy version of the true label, and the two conformal procedures degrade differently under that noise:

    • Conformal clustering stays conservative. Calibrating against a noisy label inflates the non-conformity scores, so the procedure compensates by returning more prediction sets of size 2 — i.e. it more often declines to commit to a neighborhood — rather than silently under-covering. The formal guarantee effectively still holds, at the cost of more “I don’t know” answers.
    • Conformal selection has no such built-in safety valve. Its validity relies directly on LEMUR’s predicted neighborhoods not being too wrong: if LEMUR’s assignment is systematically biased rather than just noisy, the selected neighborhood inherits that bias. In practice this means conformal selection results are only as trustworthy as the underlying LEMUR fit.

    Practical takeaway. Read a size-2 prediction set from conformal clustering as the procedure protecting itself against label noise, not as evidence that a cell has no meaningful neighborhood. Read a conformal selection result with an eye on LEMUR fit quality first — e.g. convergence diagnostics, embedding dimensionality — since that fit stands in for ground truth throughout. 

    knitr::opts_chunk$set(warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
if (!requireNamespace("conformeR", quietly = TRUE)) {
  devtools::install_github("https://github.com/juslecl/conformeR")
}
library(conformeR)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
library(knitr)

    We use a consistent, minimal theme throughout the vignette so that the conformeR plots line up visually with the tables:

    theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      legend.position = "bottom"
    )
)
conformer_palette <- c("inside" = "#4472A8", "outside" = "#D9822B", "none" = "#B0B0B0")

    Example dataset

    This vignette runs conformeR on a reduced version of the single-cell RNA-seq dataset from Zhao, Dovas, Spinazzi, et al. (2021), “Deconvolution of cell type-specific drug responses in human tumor tissue with single-cell RNA-seq,” published in Genome Medicine (GEO accession GSE148842). As with any input to conformeR, the data have already been preprocessed and quality-checked upstream.

    data("sce_vignette")
sce_vignette

rownames(sce_vignette) <- rowData(sce_vignette)$gene

    Selecting genes of interest

    We restrict the analysis to three genes with distinct expected behavior, to illustrate a range of neighborhood sizes and uncertainty patterns: HIST3H2A, PTPRZ1, and HBEGF.

    pan_affect_genes <- rowData(sce_vignette) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  dplyr::select(gid, gene) %>%
  filter(gene %in% c("HIST3H2A", "PTPRZ1", "HBEGF"))

kable(pan_affect_genes, caption = "Genes of interest for this vignette")
    Genes of interest for this vignette
    gid gene
    ENSG00000106278 PTPRZ1
    ENSG00000113070 HBEGF
    ENSG00000181218 HIST3H2A

    Running conformeR

    conformeR() fits LEMUR and layers both conformal procedures on top of it in one call. The key arguments are:

    • design_lemur — the LEMUR design formula; here we adjust for patient_id and estimate the effect of condition.
    • contrast_column — which column of the design defines the contrast of interest.
    • genes_of_interest — restrict the (more expensive) conformal layers to a gene subset; LEMUR itself is still fit genome-wide.
    • what — which conformal procedure(s) to run: "conf_selection", "conf_clustering", or both.

    By default the target coverage is cp_alpha, and the data are split 50% training / 50% calibration+test, with the calibration set taking 25 percentage points of the total (cp_train_frac and cp_cal_frac override these proportions).

    set.seed(2002)
res <- conformeR(
  sce_vignette,
  design_lemur = ~ patient_id + condition,
  contrast_column = "condition",
  genes_of_interest = pan_affect_genes$gene,
  what = c("conf_selection", "conf_clustering"),
  n_cores = 1,
  verbose = TRUE
)

    Conformal selection: how big is the affected neighborhood?

    For each gene, conformal selection returns the set of cells flagged as belonging to the neighborhood affected by condition, at the target coverage level. The table below reports both the raw neighborhood size and its share of all cells in the fitted embedding.

    selection_summary <- res$conf_results |>
  group_by(gene) |>
  summarize(
    `Neighborhood size` = sum(inside_cs),
    `% of cells` = round(sum(inside_cs) / ncol(res$fit_lemur), 2) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

kable(selection_summary, caption = "Conformal selection: neighborhood size per gene")
    Conformal selection: neighborhood size per gene
    gene Neighborhood size % of cells
    HBEGF 154 3
    HIST3H2A 374 7
    PTPRZ1 2763 55

    A larger % of cells means the gene’s condition effect is detected across a broader swath of the embedding; a small, tight neighborhood points to a more localized effect.

    Conformal clustering: how confident is each cell’s assignment?

    Conformal clustering instead reports, per cell, a prediction set: the neighborhoods that cell could plausibly belong to at the target coverage. A prediction set of size zero means the procedure could not confidently assign that cell to any neighborhood; larger sets reflect more ambiguous cells.

    clustering_summary <- res$conf_results |>
  group_by(gene) |>
  summarize(
    `Prediction set = inside`  = sum(inside_cc + outside_cc ==1 & inside_cc == 1),
    `Prediction set = outside` = sum(inside_cc + outside_cc ==1 & outside_cc == 1),
    `Prediction set size 2`    = sum(inside_cc + outside_cc !=1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

kable(clustering_summary, caption = "Conformal clustering: prediction set composition per gene")
    Conformal clustering: prediction set composition per gene
    gene Prediction set = inside Prediction set = outside Prediction set size 2
    HBEGF 551 4198 252
    HIST3H2A 1715 3005 281
    PTPRZ1 3728 986 287

    Reading this table alongside the selection table above shows where the two procedures agree (a gene with a large, confident neighborhood in both) and where they diverge (a gene with a sizeable selected neighborhood but many size-2 or ambiguous cells under clustering, which flags instability worth a closer look). Recall from the caveat above that a high count of size-2 sets is, by design, the clustering procedure’s response to calibrating against LEMUR’s noisy neighborhood labels rather than the true ones — so treat it as a built-in conservatism, not necessarily a sign that something is wrong with the gene’s effect.

    Visualizing results on the LEMUR embedding

    Conformal selection 

    plotter_conformal_selection(res, pan_affect_genes$gene)

    Conformal selection overlaid on LEMUR neighborhoods, one panel per gene.

    Cells shaded as part of the selected neighborhood are those the procedure can confidently attribute to the condition effect for that gene; unshaded cells fall outside the guaranteed selection at the chosen coverage level.

    Conformal clustering 

    plotter_conformal_clustering(res, pan_affect_genes$gene)

    Conformal prediction sets overlaid on LEMUR neighborhoods, one panel per gene.

    Here color reflects the prediction set itself rather than a single hard assignment, making it easy to spot the boundary regions where neighborhood membership is genuinely uncertain versus the core regions where every resampling agrees.
